crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
children.blurb: An AI enablement audit in finance examines how an organization prepares, deploys, and oversees AI systems across financial operations, from credit decisioning and fraud detection to reporting and customer service.

children.name: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
children.blurb: Keeping financial data out of public models concerns the controls, policies, and technical measures that prevent proprietary or regulated financial information from being used in training or fine-tuning publicly accessible AI models.

children.name: Model Risk and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Model risk and bias testing covers the formal review of quantitative models used in lending, pricing, fraud detection, capital allocation, and other financial decisions.

children.name: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
children.blurb: This page maps where financial AI systems intersect with formal rules, including prudential regulation, securities law, anti-money laundering requirements, data protection, and contractual obligations.

children.name: Local and Air-Gapped Deployment
children.blurb: Local and air-gapped deployment means running AI models and supporting systems entirely on an organization's own hardware and network, with no connection to external cloud services or the public internet.

sections.body: This field covers the controls around artificial intelligence in financial settings, from checking whether a system is actually fit to use, to stopping sensitive data from leaking into shared models, to testing for bias and model failure, to matching systems to regulations, and to running them on local or isolated hardware. In practice, AI is being used now for enablement audits that compare a model's outputs against expected accounting or compliance behavior, for scanning prompts and outputs for customer or transaction data, for statistical tests that flag skewed lending or pricing decisions, and for automated mapping of regulatory text to model documentation. The work is not theoretical; it happens inside banks, insurers, and accounting firms that already run these checks on live systems. The site tracks 210 compliance and regulation pages and 142 active AI lawsuits, which shows how much of this work is driven by real disputes and rulebooks rather than abstract risk.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The state of this work is uneven. Basic data leakage prevention, such as blocking credit card numbers or names from prompts, is fairly mature and widely deployed. Model risk and bias testing is less settled, because there is no single agreed test for fairness across lending, insurance, or audit, and many tests can be gamed or give false comfort. Regulatory mapping is still manual in many places, with teams reading rules and tagging model features by hand, though some tools now draft the first pass. Local and air-gapped deployment is technically solved for many models, but it costs more and often means older or smaller models, so firms trade capability for control. The honest limit is that no audit or test can prove a model is safe, only that known failure modes were checked on a given day.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with The AI Enablement Audit in Finance to see what a practical pre-deployment and ongoing review looks like, then move to Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models for the specific controls around prompts, training data, and output filters. Model Risk and Bias Testing goes deeper into the statistical and behavioral checks that follow an enablement audit. Mapping Financial AI to the Rules connects those checks to actual laws, standards, and regulator expectations, which is where many teams get stuck. Local and Air-Gapped Deployment covers the infrastructure side, for readers who need to run models without sending data to a third party. Together the five pages move from deciding whether to use a model, to protecting the data, to testing the model, to proving compliance, and finally to running it in a controlled environment.
